# L7: [summaries and import/export in tidyverse]{.flow} {#clase-0-7}


## count()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |> count(var1, var2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |> count(var1, var2)
```
:::
:::

So far we have only transformed or queried the data but we have not generated statistics. Let's start with the simple: [**how to count (frequencies)?**]{.hl-yellow}

. . .

When used alone `count()` will simply return the number of records, but when used with `count()` variables it calculates what is known as [**frequencies**]{.hl-yellow}: [**number of elements of each modality**]{.hl-purple}.

```{r}
starwars |> count(sex)
```

---

## count()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |> count(var1, var2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |> count(var1, var2)
```
:::
:::

Also if we pass several variables it calculates what is known as a [**contiguity table**]{.hl-yellow}. With `sort = TRUE` it will return the [**ordered count**]{.hl-purple} (most frequent first).


```{r}
starwars |> count(sex, gender, sort = TRUE)
```

---

## group_by()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |>
  group(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  group_by(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::
:::

One of the most powerful [**functions**]{.hl-yellow} to combine with the actions seen is `group_by()`, which will allow us to [**group our records**]{.hl-yellow} beforehand.


```{r}
starwars |> 
  group_by(sex) |>
  count() |>
  ungroup()
```

---

## group_by()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |>
  group(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  group_by(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::
:::

When applying `group_by()` it is important to understand that it [**DOES NOT MODIFY the data**]{.hl-yellow}, but creates a [**group variable**]{.hl-yellow} (sub-tables for each group) that will modify future actions: the [**operations will be applied to each sub-table separately**]{.hl-purple}

. . .

For example, imagine that we want to extract the highest character with `slice_max()`.

```{r}
starwars |> slice_max(height)
```


---

## group_by()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |>
  group(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  group_by(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::
:::

What if we want to [**extract the tallest character but...of each of the sexes**]{.hl-yellow}?

. . .

```{r}
starwars |>
  group_by(sex) |> 
  slice_max(height) |> 
  ungroup()
```

---

## group_by()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |>
  group(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  group_by(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::
:::

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/tidydatatutor_1.jpg)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/tidydatatutor_2.jpg)
:::
:::

The web <https://tidydatatutor.com/> allows to visualize the operations of `{tidyverse}` (doing with the old pipe `%>%`)

---

## group_by()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |>
  group(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |> 
  ungroup()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  group_by(var1, var2) |> 
  some_action() |>
  ungroup()
```
:::
:::

::: callout-important
## Important

You should always remember to [**make ungroup**]{.hl-red} to remove the created group variable.

:::

. . .

The "new" version of `{dplyr}` now [**allows to include the group variable**]{.hl-yellow} in the call to many functions with the argument `by = ...` or `.by = ...`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |> slice_max(height, by = sex)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
starwars |> slice_max(height, by = sex) |> select(name:eye_color)
```

---

## Row-by-row: rowwise()

A very useful option used before an operation is also `rowwise()`: every [**operation that comes afterwards will be applied on each row separately**]{.hl-yellow}. For example, let's define a dummy set of grades.

```{r}
grades <- tibble("maths" = c(7.5, 8, 9.1, 3),
                 "language" = c(8, 6, 6.5, 9.2))
```

. . .

If we apply the average directly the value will be identical since it has done the global average, but we would like to get an [**average per record**]{.hl-yellow}. For that we will use `rowwise()`.

```{r}
grades |> 
  rowwise() |> 
  mutate(ave_grades = mean(c(maths, language)))
```

---

## Summary: summarise()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |> simple_summary()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |> summarise()
```
:::
:::

Finally we have `summarise()`, which will allow us to get statistical summaries. For example, let's [**calculate the average of the heights**]{.hl-yellow}.

```{r}
starwars |> 
  drop_na(height) |> 
  summarise(ave_height = mean(height))
```

. . .

::: callout-warning
##  Be careful

Notice that `mutate()` returns [**as many rows as original records**]{.hl-yellow}, while with `summarise()` it calculates a [**new summary dataset**]{.hl-purple}, only including what is indicated.

:::

---

## Summary: summarise()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |> simple_summary()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |> summarise()
```
:::
:::

If we also [**combine this with the grouping**]{.hl-yellow} of `group_by()` or `.by = ...`, in a few lines of code you can get [**disaggregated statistics**]{.hl-purple}.

```{r}
starwars |> 
  drop_na(sex, height, mass) |> 
  summarise(ave_height = mean(height),
            ave_mass = mean(mass),
            .by = sex)
```

---

## Summary: reframe()

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
data |> complex_summary()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
starwars |> reframe()
```
:::
:::

In the new `{dplyr}` they have included `reframe()` to avoid `summarise()` problems when [**we return more than one value per variable**]{.hl-yellow} in more complex summaries.


::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| warning: true
starwars |>
  drop_na(mass) |>
  summarise(quantile(mass))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
starwars |>
  drop_na(mass) |>
  reframe(quantile(mass))
```
:::
:::

---

## across()

One trick is to [**make use of selectors**]{.hl-yellow} `across()` and `where()`. The former allows us to [**act on several columns by name**]{.hl-purple} (with `mutate()` or `summarise()`).


```{r}
starwars |> summarise(ave = across(height:mass, mean, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sex)
```

. . .

The second, `where()`, allows us to do the same but [**selecting by type**]{.hl-yellow}.

```{r}
starwars |> 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), mean, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(sex, gender))
```


---

### [**Exercise 1**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Calculate how many characters there are of each species, ordered from most to least frequent.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false
starwars |> count(species, sort = TRUE)
```

### [**Exercise 2**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 After eliminating missing variables for weight and height, add a new variable to calculate the BMI of each character, and determine the average BMI of our characters disaggregated by gender.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  drop_na(mass, height) |> 
  mutate(BMI = mass / ((height/100)^2)) |> 
  summarise(ave_BMI = mean(BMI), .by = sex)
```

### [**Exercise 3**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Obtain the youngest character for each gender.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false
starwars |> # reminder that birth_year is in fact the age
  slice_min(birth_year, by = sex)
```

### [**Exercise 4**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Get the age of the youngest and oldest character of each sex.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  drop_na(birth_year) |>
  summarise(min(birth_year), max(birth_year), .by = sex)
```

### [**Exercise 5**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Determine the number of characters in each decade (take a look at `round()`, first without disaggregating and then disaggregated by sex.

```{r}

starwars |>
  count(birth_decade = round(birth_year, -1))
```

## Import/export

So far we have only used data already loaded in packages but many times [**we will need to import data externally**]{.hl-yellow}. One of the main [**strengths**]{.hl-yellow} of `R` is that we can import data very easily in different formats:


* [**R native formats**]{.hl-yellow}: `.rda`, `.RData` and `.rds` formats.

* [**Rectangular (tabular) data**]{.hl-yellow}: `.csv` and `.tsv` formats

* [**Untabulated data**]{.hl-yellow}: `.txt` format.

* [**Data in excel**]{.hl-yellow}: `.xls` and `.xlsx` formats

* [**Data from SAS/Stata/SPSS**]{.hl-yellow}: `.sas7bdat`, `.sav` and `.dat` formats

* [**Data from Google Drive**]{.hl-yellow}

* [**Data from API's**]{.hl-yellow}: aemet, catastro, twitter, spotify, etc.

---

## R native formats

The [**simplest**]{.hl-yellow} files to import into `R` (and which usually take up less disk space) are its own [**native extensions**]{.hl-yellow}: files in `.RData`, `.rda` and `.rds` formats. To load the former we simply need to [**use the native**]{.hl-yellow} function `load()` by providing it the file path.

* `RData` file: we are going to import the file `world_bank_pop.RData`, which includes the dataset `world_bank_pop`


```{r}
load("./data/world_bank_pop.RData")
world_bank_pop
```


---

## R native formats

* `.rda` file: we will import the airquality dataset from `airquality.rda`

```{r}
load("./data/airquality.rda")
airquality |> as_tibble()
```

---

## R native formats

Note that files loaded with `load()` are [**automatically loaded into the environment**]{.hl-yellow} (with the originally saved name), and not only datasets can be loaded: `load()` allows us to load multiple objetcs (not only a tabular data)

Native `.rda` and `.RData` files are a properly way to save your environment.

```{r}
#| eval: false
load(file = "./data/multiple_objects.rda")
```


---

## R native formats

* `.rds` files: for this type we must use `readRDS()`, and we need to incorporate a [**argument `file`**]{.hl-yellow} with the path. In this case we are going to import [**lung cancer data**]{.hl-purple} from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group. Note that now [**.rds import files are a unique database**]{.hl-yellow}

```{r}
#| eval: false
lung_cancer <-
  readRDS(file = "./data/NCCTG_lung_cancer.rds") |>
  as_tibble()
```


::: callout-important

## Important

The [**paths**]{.hl-yellow} must always be [**without spaces, ñ, or accents**]{.hl-yellow}. 

:::

---

## Tabular data: readr

The `{readr}` package within the `{tidyverse}` environment contains several useful functions for [**loading rectangular data (without formatting)**]{.hl-yellow}.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

* `read_csv()`: `.csv` files whose [**separator is comma**]{.hl-purple}
* `read_csv2()`: [**semicolon**]{.hl-purple}
* `read_tsv()`: [**tabulator**]{.hl-purple}.
* `read_table()`: [**space**]{.hl-purple}.
* `read_delim()`: generic function for [**character delimited files**]{.hl-purple}.


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](img/data-import-readr.png)
:::
::::

All of them need as **argument the file path** plus **other optional** (skip header or not, decimals, etc). See more at <https://readr.tidyverse.org/>

---

## Tabular data (.csv, .tsv)

The main advantage of `{readr}` is that it [**automates formatting**]{.hl-yellow} to go from a flat (unformatted) file to a tibble (in rows and columns, with formatting).

. . .

* File `.csv`: with `read_csv()` we will load [**comma separated**]{.hl-purple} files, passing as [**argument the path**]{.hl-yellow} in `file = ...`. Let's import the `chickens.csv` dataset (about cartoon chickens, why not). If you look at the output it gives us the type of variables.

```{r}
library(readr)
chickens <- read_csv(file = "./data/chickens.csv")
chickens
```

---

## Tabular data (.csv, .tsv)


The [**variable format**]{.hl-yellow} will normally be done [**automatically**]{.hl-yellow} by `read_csv()`, and we can query it with `spec()`.

```{r}
spec(chickens)
```

---

## Tabular data (.csv, .tsv)

Although it usually does it well automatically we can [**specify the format explicitly**]{.hl-yellow} in `col_types = list()` (in list format, with `col_xxx()` for each type of variable, for example `eggs_laid` will be imported as character). 


```{r}
chickens <-
  read_csv(file = "./data/chickens.csv",
           col_types = list(col_character(), col_character(),
                            col_character(), col_character()))
chickens
```

---

## Tabular data (.csv, .tsv)

We can even indicate that [**variables we want to select**]{.hl-yellow} (without occupying memory), by indicating it in `col_select = ...` (in list format, with `col_select = ...`).


```{r}
chickens <-
  read_csv(file = "./data/chickens.csv",
           col_select = c(chicken, sex, eggs_laid))
chickens
```

---

## Untabulated data (.txt)

What happens when the [**separator is not correct**]{.hl-red}?

. . .

If we use `read_csv()` it expects the separator between columns to be a comma but, as you can see with the following `.txt`, it interprets everything as a single column: [**has no comma and does not know where to separate**]{.hl-yellow}

```{r}
datos_txt <- read_csv(file = "./data/massey-rating.txt")
dim(datos_txt)
as_tibble(datos_txt)
```


---

## Untabulated data (.txt)

To do this we have.

* `read_csv2()` when the [**separator is semicolon**]{.hl-yellow}, `read_tsv()` when the [**is a tab**]{.hl-yellow} and `read_table()` when the [**is a space**]{.hl-yellow}.

* `read_delim()` in general.

```{r}
datos_txt <- read_table(file = "./data/massey-rating.txt")
as_tibble(datos_txt)
```


---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)

Another key import package will be the `{readxl}` package for [**importing data from Excel**]{.hl-yellow}. Three functions will be key:

* `read_xls()` specific to `.xls`, `read_xlsx()` specific to `.xlsx`.
* `read_excel()`: for both `.xls` and `.xlsx`.

. . .

We are going to import `deaths.xlsx` with celebrity death records.

```{r}
library(readxl)
deaths <- read_xlsx(path = "./data/deaths.xlsx")
deaths
```

---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)


```{r}
deaths |> slice(1:6)
```

One thing that is [**very common misfortune**]{.hl-yellow} is that there is some kind of comment or text at the beginning of the file, having to [**skip those rows**]{.hl-yellow}.

---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)

We can [**skip these rows**]{.hl-yellow} directly in the load with `skip = ...` (indicating the number of rows to skip).

```{r}
deaths <- read_xlsx(path = "./data/deaths.xlsx", skip = 4)
deaths
```


---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)

In addition with `col_names = ...` we can already rename the columns in the import (if [**provide names assumes 1st line already as a data**]{.hl-yellow})

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "2-3"
deaths <-
  read_xlsx(path = "./data/deaths.xlsx", skip = 5,
            col_names = c("name", "profession", "age", "kids", "birth", "death"))
deaths
```

---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)

Sometimes [**Excel dates are incorrectly formatted**]{.hl-red} (surprise): we can use `convertToDate()` from the `{openxlsx}` package to convert it.


```{r}
library(openxlsx)
deaths$death <- convertToDate(deaths$death)
deaths
```
   

---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)

We can also [**load an Excel with several sheets**]{.hl-yellow}: to [**indicate the sheet**]{.hl-yellow} (either by its name or by its number) we will use the argument `sheet = ...`.

```{r}
mtcars <- read_xlsx(path = "./data/datasets.xlsx", sheet = "mtcars")
mtcars
```

---

## Excel data (.xls, .xlsx)

 
We can even indicate the [**range of cells**]{.hl-yellow} to load with `range = ...`.

```{r}
iris <- read_xlsx(path = "./data/datasets.xlsx", sheet = "iris", range = "C1:E4")
iris
```

---

## Import from SAS/STATA/SPSS

The `{haven}` package within the tidyverse orbit will allow us to [**import files from the 3 most important payment software**]{.hl-yellow}: SAS, SPSS and Stata.

```{r}
library(haven)

# SAS
iris_sas <- read_sas(data_file = "./data/iris.sas7bdat")

# SPSS
iris_spss <- read_sav(file = "./data/iris.sav")

# Stata
iris_stata <- read_dta(file = "./data/iris.dta")
```


---


## Export

In the same way that we can import we can also [**export**]{.hl-yellow}

* exported in `.RData` (recommended option for variables stored in `R`). Remember that this extension [**can only be used in `R`**]{.hl-yellow}. To do so, just use `save(object, file = path)`.

```{r}
table <- tibble("a" = 1:4, "b" = 1:4)
save(table, file = "./data/table.RData")
rm(table) # eliminar
load("./data/table.RData")
table
```

---

## Export

In the same way that we can import we can also [**export**]{.hl-yellow}

* exported in `.RData` multiple objects

```{r}
table <- tibble("a" = 1:4, "b" = 1:4)
a <- 1
b <- c("javi", "sandra")
save(table, a, b, file = "./data/mult_obj.RData")
rm(list = c("a", "b", "table"))
load("./data/mult_obj.RData")
table
```

---

## Export

In the same way that we can import we can also [**export**]{.hl-yellow}

* exported in `.csv`. To do this we simply use `write_csv(object, file = path)`.

```{r}
write_csv(table, file = "./data/table.csv")
read_csv(file = "./data/table.csv")
```

---

## Import from website

One of the main advantages of `R` is that we can make use of all the previous functions of [**import but directly from a web**]{.hl-yellow}, without the need to perform the manual download: instead of passing it the local path we will indicate the [**link**]{.hl-yellow}. For example, we are going to download the covid data from ISCIII (<https://cnecovid.isciii.es/covid19/#documentaci%C3%B3n-y-datos>)

```{r}
#| eval: false
covid_data <-
  read_csv(file = "https://cnecovid.isciii.es/covid19/resources/casos_hosp_uci_def_sexo_edad_provres.csv")
covid_data
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
covid_data <-
  read_csv(file = "https://cnecovid.isciii.es/covid19/resources/casos_hosp_uci_def_sexo_edad_provres.csv", n_max = 500)
covid_data
```

---

## Import from wikipedia

The `{rvest}` package, one of the most useful of `{tidyverse}` allows us to import directly from an `html`. For example, to export wikipedia tables just `read_html()` to import the html, `html_element("table")` to extract the table objects, and `html_table()` to convert the html table to `tibble`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(rvest)
wiki_jump <- 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men%27s_long_jump_world_record_progression'
wiki_jump |> read_html() |> 
  html_element("table") |> 
  html_table()
```

---


## Import from google drive

Another option available (especially if we work with other people working) is to [**import from a Google Drive spreadsheet**]{.hl-yellow}, making use of `read_sheet()` from the `{googlesheets4}` package.

The first time you will be asked for a tidyverse permission to interact with your drive

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(googlesheets4)
google_sheet <-
  read_sheet("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Uz38nHjl3bmftxDpcXj--DYyPo1I39NHVf-xjeg1_wI/edit?usp=sharing")
google_sheet
```

---

## Import from API (owid)

Another interesting option is the [**data download from an API**]{.hl-yellow}: an intermediary between an app or data provider and our `R`. For example, let's load the `{owidR}` library, which allows us to download data from the web <https://ourworldindata.org/>. For example, the `owid_covid()` function loads without realizing it more than 400 000 records with more than 60 variables from 238 countries.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(owidR)
owid_covid() |> as_tibble()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
library(owidR)
owid_covid() |> as_tibble() |> slice(1:7)
```

---

In many occasions to connect to the API we will first have to [**register and obtain a key**]{.hl-yellow}, this is the case of the `{climaemet}` package to access [**Spanish meteorological data**]{.hl-yellow} (<https://opendata.aemet.es/centrodedescargas/inicio>).

```{r}
aemet_api_key(apikey, install = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false

```

## Import from API (aemet)


With this package we can do a [**search for stations**]{.hl-yellow} to know both its postal code and its identifier code within the AEMET network

```{r}
#| eval: false
stations <- aemet_stations()
stations
```

---

## Import from API (aemet)

For example, to get data from the station of the airport of El Prat, Barcelona, the code to provide is `"0076"`, obtaining **hourly data**

```{r}
#| eval: false
aemet_last_obs("0076")
```


---


## Importar from API (US census)

One of the most useful tools in recent years is known as `{tidycensus}`: a tool for [**facilitating the process of downloading census data**]{.hl-yellow} for the United States from `R`.

```{r}
library(tidycensus)
```

* `get_decennial()`: to access the [**census data (US Decennial Census)**]{.hl-yellow}, done every 10 years (years 2000, 2010 and 2020).

* `get_acs()`: to access the [**annual and quinquennial (5 years) ACS (American Community Survey)**]{.hl-yellow} (census != survey)

* `get_estimates()`: to access the [**annual population, birth and death estimates**]{.hl-yellow} (census != survey)

* `get_pums()`: to access the [**microdata (unaggregated data) of the ACS (anonymized at the individual level)**]{.hl-yellow}

* `get_flows()`: to access the [**migration flow**]{.hl-yellow} data.


---

## Importar from API (US census)

For example, we will download the **census data** (`get_decennial()`) at the state level (`geography = “state”`) for the population (variable `variables = “P001001”`) for the year 2010 (see variables in `tidycensus::load_variables()`).

```{r}
#| eval: false
total_population_10 <-
  get_decennial(geography = "state", 
  variables = "P001001",
  year = 2010)
total_population_10
```



---

## Import from API 

Other options:

* `{chessR}`: data from chess matches. See <https://github.com/JaseZiv/chessR>

* `{spotifyr}`: data from Spotify. See <https://www.rcharlie.com/spotifyr/>

* `{gtrendsR}`: data from Google Trends. See <https://github.com/PMassicotte/gtrendsR>

* `{scholar}`: data from <https://github.com/jkeirstead/scholar>

# MODULE 2: applied statistics in R {#module-2}


# L1: [introduction to ggplot]{.flow} {#clase-1-1}



[**Introduction to ggplot: dataviz is not just a pretty tool**]{style="color:#444442;"}

* [📆 Planning](#planificacion-2)

---

## Statistics in R

💡 [**Core idea**]{.hl-yellow}

> Before modeling, inferring, or testing… we need to understand the data. And that starts by looking at it

. . .

🎯 Why is **visualization key in statistics**?

. . .

1. It **reveals** what numbers hide
2. It **helps** identify patterns and relationships
3. It **detects** errors and outliers, helping with data cleaning
4. It helps **formulate hypotheses**, even though a graph alone cannot confirm or reject them
5. Analysis doesn’t end with results: what is not **communicated** does not exist

---

## Example

1. Get into **groups** until you form 4 teams. Each team should download a `.csv` file (click [here](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/17TJJKu6vhcEfb99LtiVZZtTCy6xQ4DXf?usp=sharing))

. . .

2. Each team should **import their file** by placing the `.csv` inside the RStudio project and loading it into R **as a tibble**.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dataset_1 <- anscombe |> as_tibble() |> select(x1, y1)
dataset_2 <- anscombe |> as_tibble() |> select(x2, y2)
dataset_3 <- anscombe |> as_tibble() |> select(x3, y3)
dataset_4 <- anscombe |> as_tibble() |> select(x4, y4)
```

. . .

3. Create a **summary table** similar to the one below by calculating the mean of x and y, the variance of x and y, and their correlation.

```{r}
#| echo: false
dataset_1 |>
  summarise("mean_x" = mean(x1), "mean_y" = mean(y1),
            "var_x" = var(x1), "var_y" = var(y1),
            "cor_xy" = cor(x1, y1))
```

. . .

4. Share the results from each group with the class. **What conclusions do you draw?**

---

## Example


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
dataset_1 |>
  summarise("mean_x" = mean(x1), "mean_y" = mean(y1),
            "var_x" = var(x1), "var_y" = var(y1),
            "cor_xy" = cor(x1, y1)) |> 
  mutate("dataset" = "dataset_1") |> 
  bind_rows(dataset_2 |>
              summarise("mean_x" = mean(x2), "mean_y" = mean(y2),
                        "var_x" = var(x2), "var_y" = var(y2),
                        "cor_xy" = cor(x2, y2)) |> 
              mutate("dataset" = "dataset_2")) |> 
  bind_rows(dataset_3 |>
              summarise("mean_x" = mean(x3), "mean_y" = mean(y3),
                        "var_x" = var(x3), "var_y" = var(y3),
                        "cor_xy" = cor(x3, y3)) |> 
              mutate("dataset" = "dataset_3")) |> 
  bind_rows(dataset_4 |>
              summarise("mean_x" = mean(x4), "mean_y" = mean(y4),
                        "var_x" = var(x4), "var_y" = var(y4),
                        "cor_xy" = cor(x4, y4)) |> 
              mutate("dataset" = "dataset_4"))
```

**ALL** the summary measures are identical to the first decimal place → [**Are the four datasets essentially the same?**]{.hl-orange}

---

## Example

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(showtext)
library(sysfonts)

font_add_google("Space Grotesk", "space")
showtext_auto()
theme_own <- 
  theme_minimal(base_family = "space") + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 17),
        plot.subtitle =
          element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, color = "grey30"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 13))

datasets <-
  dataset_1 |> 
  rename(x = x1, y = y1) |> 
  mutate("dataset" = "dataset_1") |> 
  bind_rows(dataset_2 |> 
              rename(x = x2, y = y2) |> 
              mutate("dataset" = "dataset_2")) |> 
  bind_rows(dataset_3 |> 
              rename(x = x3, y = y3) |> 
              mutate("dataset" = "dataset_3")) |> 
  bind_rows(dataset_4 |> 
              rename(x = x4, y = y4) |> 
              mutate("dataset" = "dataset_4"))
ggplot(datasets,
       aes(x = x, y = y, color = dataset)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, size = 4.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~dataset) +
  theme_own +
  labs(color = "dataset", 
       title = "Are the same dataset?",
       subtitle = "Datasets extracted from the well-known Anscombe's Quartet. All datasets fit the same regression line")
```

---

## Dataviz: not only a pretty tool

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
library(datasauRus)
datasaurus_dozen |> 
  summarise("mean_x" = mean(x), "mean_y" = mean(y), "cor_xy" = cor(x, y),
            .by = dataset)
```


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(datasauRus)
ggplot(datasaurus_dozen |> 
         filter(dataset != "v_lines"),
       aes(x = x, y = y, color = dataset)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  MetBrewer::scale_color_met_d(palette_name = "Renoir") +
  facet_wrap(~ dataset, ncol = 3) +
  theme_own +
  labs(title = "Datasaurus dozen dataset")
```

---


## Dataviz: a bit of history


The emergence of statistical graphics is [**relatively recent in science**]{.hl-yellow}, since until the Middle Ages the only visualizations were **maps**

:::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

It was when [**navigation and astronomy**]{.hl-yellow} began to gain importance that the first graph (not strictly statistical) appeared, depicting the cyclical movement of the planets (10th–11th centuries).

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/dataviz_historico_1.png){width="370"}
:::
::::
 

. . .

Most experts, such as Tufte [^3] [^4], consider this nearly longitudinal chart as the [**first data visualization**]{.hl-yellow} in history, created by Van Langren in 1644, showing the **distance between Toledo and Rome**

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("./img/longitud_dataviz.jpg")
``` 

::: {style="font-size:60%"}

[^1]: [«Gramática de las gráficas: pistas para mejorar las representaciones de datos» de Joaquín Sevilla](http://academica-e.unavarra.es/bitstream/handle/2454/15785/Gram%C3%A1tica.pdf)

[^2]: [«Quantitative Graphics in Statistics: A Brief History» de James R. Beniger y Dorothy L. Robyn. The American Statistician (1978)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2683467)]

[^3]: [«Visual explanations: images and quantities, evidence and narrative» de E. Tufte](https://archive.org/details/visualexplanatio00tuft)

[^4]: [«PowerPoint is evil» de E. Tufte](https://www.wired.com/2003/09/ppt2/)

:::

---

## Dataviz: a bit of history

In the 17th century, there was a boom in statistics as it began to be applied to [**demography**]{.hl-yellow}. One of the most important authors was J. Graunt, author of Natural and Political Observations Made upon the Bills of Mortality (1662), who estimated the population of London using the [**first birth and death tables**]{.hl-yellow}.

However, the figure who truly transformed data visualization was, without a doubt, the economist and politician [**William Playfair (1759–1823)**]{.hl-yellow}, who in 1786 published the **Political and Commercial Atlas** featuring 44 charts (including the most famous bar chart in history).


```{r echo = FALSE, out.width = "30%", fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Extracted from Funkhouser and Walker (1935)"}
knitr::include_graphics("./img/playfair_6.jpg")
``` 




[^5]: [«Atlas político y comercial» de William Playfair (1786)](https://www.amazon.es/Playfairs-Commercial-Political-Statistical-Breviary/dp/0521855543)

[^6]: [«Playfair and his charts» de H. Gray Funkhouser and  Helen M. Walker (1935)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/45366440)


---


## What is a dataviz?


Is this a statistical dataviz? Why or why not?

![](img/cuadro_dataviz.jpg)


. . .

There is [**no INFORMATION**]{.hl-red} represented.

---

## What is a dataviz?

Is this a statistical dataviz? Why or why not?


![](img/celsius_dataviz.jpg)

. . .

There is [**no DATA**]{.hl-red} represented (just a physical magnitude and its conversion, just a formula)

---

## What is a dataviz?

These same questions were posed by **Joaquín Sevilla** [^7 ], who provided [**3 requirements**]{.hl-yellow}:

1. It must be based on the [**metric axis**]{.hl-yellow} framework (measurement process): it must [**measure something**]{.hl-yellow}.
2. It must include [**statistical information (data)**]{.hl-yellow}.
3. The [**representational relationship**]{.hl-yellow} must be [**reversible**]{.hl-purple}: the data should be able to be “recovered” from the chart.

[^7]: [«Gramática de las gráficas: pistas para mejorar las representaciones de datos» de Joaquín Sevilla](http://academica-e.unavarra.es/bitstream/handle/2454/15785/Gram%C3%A1tica.pdf)

---

## Vizfails

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](img/persona_dataviz.jpg)
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

* The chosen figure (person walking) has no relation to what is being visualized: [**poor metaphor**]{.hl-red}.

* The [**marked sectors have no relation to the item**]{.hl-red} being represented, making interpretation difficult.

* The [**colors are uncoded**]{.hl-red}: they provide no information.

* The [**irregular shapes prevent comparison**]{.hl-red} of areas (also, the total exceeds 100%).

* No source provided

:::
::::

## Vizfails

![](img/viz_fail_covid.jpg)

## Context is crucial

A **good idea can be poorly executed**: how it is implemented matters.

## Dataviz in R: ggplot2

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

The `{ggplot2}` package is based on [**«Grammar of graphics»**]{.hl-yellow} by Leland Wilkinson: giving graphics their own grammar.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
```

[**Data visualization**]{.hl-yellow} should be a fundamental part of any data analysis. It’s not just about aesthetics.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/telling_dataviz.jpg){width="400"}
:::
:::

---

## Dataviz in R: ggplot2

The goal is to start with a blank canvas and gradually [**add layers to your plot**]{.hl-yellow}, just like you would in Photoshop. The advantage of {ggplot2} is that it allows you to [**map aesthetic attributes**]{.hl-purple} (color, shape, size) of geometric objects (points, bars, lines) **based on the data**.

You can check the **package documentation** here: <https://ggplot2-book.org/introduction.html>


![](img/grammar_ggplot2.jpg)

---

## Dataviz in R: ggplot2

![](img/tarta_ggplot2.png)

---

## Dataviz in R: ggplot2

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/tarta_recortada_ggplot2.jpg)
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

A figure can be composed of [**layers**]{.hl-yellow}:

- [**Data**]{.hl-purple}
- [**Aesthetics (mapping)**]{.hl-purple}: visual elements such as axes, color, shape, etc. (mapped from the data)
- [**Geometries (geom)**]{.hl-purple}: points, lines, bars, polygons, etc.
- [**Faceting (facet)**]{.hl-purple}: splitting plots into multiple panels
- [**Statistical transformations (stat)**]{.hl-purple}: ordering, summarizing, etc.
- [**Coordinates (coord)**]{.hl-purple}: Cartesian, polar, grids, etc.
- [**Themes (theme)**]{.hl-purple}: fonts, text size, subtitles, captions, legends, axes, etc.

:::
:::

---


## First attempt

Let’s look at a **first attempt** to understand the ggplot philosophy. For this, we’ll use the `gapminder` dataset from the package of the same name: a file containing **life expectancy, population, and per capita income data for different countries**.

**Task**: the file contains 1,704 records and 6 variables (`country`, `continent`, `year`, `lifeExp`, `pop`, and `gdpPercap`). [**Filter only the 2007 data**]{.hl-yellow} and remove missing values from `lifeExp`, `pop`, and `gdpPercap`.


```{r}
library(gapminder)
gapminder
```


```{r}
#| echo: false
gapminder_2007 <-
  gapminder |> 
  filter(year == 2007) |> 
  drop_na(lifeExp, pop, gdpPercap)
```


---


## Canvas

What [**elements do we need**]{.hl-yellow} to create a plot? To [**start the canvas**]{.hl-purple}, we need a dataset and a call to `ggplot()`.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}

* [**Instruction**]{.hl-yellow}: `ggplot()` 
* [**Data**]{.hl-yellow}: dataset `gapminder_2007`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007)

# alternative
gapminder_2007 |> 
  ggplot()
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007)
```

:::
::::

---

## Which plot?

In our case, we want to see the relationship between `gdpPercap` and `pop`. **What plot would you make** and why?

. . .

The most immediate and simple option is the well-known [**scatter plot**]{.hl-yellow}, and for this we need to [**tell ggplot() which GEOMETRY**]{.hl-yellow} (type) we want to use.


:::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}

* **Instruction**: `ggplot()` 
* **Data**: dataset `gapminder_2007`.
* [**Geometry (geom_)**]{.hl-yellow}: we chose **scatter** using `geom_point()`.  **Variables should be cuantitative (continuous)**.


```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point()
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| error: true
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point()
```

:::
::::

. . .

Notice the error: [**«requires the following missing aesthetics: x and y»**]{.hl-red}. We have the data and the type of plot, but... **which variables should we use?**

---


## Ingredients: (x, y)


In this case, we want `gdpPercap` to be on the X-axis and `pop` on the Y-axis. Here’s the main tool of `ggplot`: we can specify inside `geom_point()` that the [**aesthetic attributes**]{.hl-yellow} of the plot `(x, y)` depend on [**data attributes/variables**]{.hl-purple} (`gdpPercap` and `pop`)

:::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}

* **Instruction**: `ggplot()` 
* **Data**: dataset `gapminder_2007`.
* **Geometry (geom_)**: we chose **scatter** using `geom_point()`.
* [**Mapping (aes)**]{.hl-yellow}: what is x? what is y? Everything inside [**`aes()` will be mapped from the table**]{.hl-green}


```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(data = gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap,
                 y = pop))
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = pop))
```

:::
::::

---

## Think about it again

```{r}
ggplot(gapminder_2007) + geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = pop))
```

* Canvas: `ggplot()` + data
* Geometry: what type of plot do I want?
* `aes()`: which aspects of my geometry should depend on the data?

. . .

**What would you need to change** in the code if we want to make a scatter plot with pop on the X-axis and gdpPercap on the Y-axis?

---

## Think about it again

```{r}
ggplot(gapminder_2007) + geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap, x = pop))
```

* Canvas: `ggplot()` + data
* Geometry: what type of plot do I want?
* `aes()`: which aspects of my geometry should depend on the data?

. . .

**What would you need to change** in the code if we want to make a scatter plot with gdpPercap on the X-axis and life expectancy on the Y-axis?


---

## Think about it again

```{r}
ggplot(gapminder_2007) + geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))
```

* Canvas: `ggplot()` + data
* Geometry: what type of plot do I want?
* `aes()`: which aspects of my geometry should depend on the data?


---

## More geometries

What **other types of plots** can you think of to represent `gdpPercap`, `lifeExp`, or `pop`? (separately)

. . .

* [**Histograms**]{.hl-red}: often not ideal because they depend on a subjective decision like the number of bins
* [**Density plots**]{.hl-yellow}: very useful to see the data distribution (and to form a hypothesis about whether they are normal or not)
* [**Boxplots**]{.hl-orange}: very common in research to show data relative to the median and percentiles, and to detect outliers

. . .

**What would need to be changed** in this code to switch to a different type of plot?

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))
```

---

## More geometries

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_density(aes(x = lifeExp))
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(y = gdpPercap))
```

:::

::::

---

## Color, size, shape

We come back to `geom_point()`. Could we **customize** any other elements?

. . .

* `color = ...`: color (if mapped to a variable, it changes the outline; otherwise, it sets the point color)

* `fill = ...`: fill color


:::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

We’ll start with a [**fixed color**]{.hl-yellow}, for example "red" (others include "blue", "black", "yellow", etc.).

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap,
                 x = lifeExp),
             color = "red")
```

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")
```

:::
::::


---


## Color, size, shape

:::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

* `size = ...`: size of geometry (in that case, **size of points**)

  
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap,
                 x = lifeExp),
             color = "red", size = 6) 
```

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 6)
```

:::
::::

---

## Color, size, shape


:::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

* `alpha = ...`: % of opacity (1 completely fill, 0 completely transparent)

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp),
             color = "red", size = 6, alpha = 0.4)
```

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 6, alpha = 0.4)
```

:::
::::

---

## Color, size, shape


:::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

* `shape = ...`: shape of geometry (point, square, diamond, triangle, ...). See all of them in `vignette("ggplot2-specs")`


```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap,
                 x = lifeExp),
             color = "red",
             fill = "black",
             size = 6,
             alpha = 0.4,
             shape = 23)
```

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(color = "red", fill = "black",
             size = 6, alpha = 0.4, shape = 23)
```

:::
::::

---

## Color, size, shape


:::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

* `stroke = ...`: width of contour.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap,
                 x = lifeExp),
             color = "red",
             fill = "black",
             size = 6,
             alpha = 0.4,
             stroke = 3)
```

:::

::: {.column width=60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(color = "red", fill = "black", alpha = 0.4,
             size = 6, stroke = 3)
```

:::
::::


---

## About colors


:::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}

We can also **assign colors using their hexadecimal code**, which you can look up at <https://htmlcolorcodes.com/es/> to choose any color you want. The hexadecimal code always starts with `#`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap,
                 x = lifeExp),
             color = "#A02B85",
             alpha = 0.4,
             size = 6) 
```


:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(color = "#A02B85", alpha = 0.4, size = 6)
```

:::
::::

  
---

## More variables: aes()


So far, we have passed the **aesthetic attributes** as fixed and [**constant**]{.hl-yellow} except axis. But the true power and versatility of ggplot is that we can [**map ALL attributes based on the data**]{.hl-yellow} inside `aes()` so that they depend on variables from the dataset.

&nbsp;

[**How we can include more variables in the scatter plot?**]{.hl-orange}

---

## More variables: aes()


[**How we can include more variables in the scatter plot?**]{.hl-orange}


:::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}

For example, let’s assign a [**color to each data point based on its continent**]{.hl-yellow} using `aes(color = continent)`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp,
                 color = continent),
             size = 5)
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(size = 5)
```

:::
::::

---

## More variables: aes()


:::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
  
We can combine it with what we did before:

* [**color**]{.hl-yellow} based on [**continent**]{.hl-purple}
* [**size**]{.hl-yellow} based on [**population**]{.hl-purple}
* [**transparency**]{.hl-yellow} set to a [**constant**]{.hl-purple} of 50%

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap,
                 x = lifeExp,
                 color = continent,
                 size = pop),
             alpha = 0.7)
```

This particular scatter plot is known as a **BUBBLE CHART**

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp,
           color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7)
```

:::
::::



---

## Think about it
  
Let’s think about the previous plot:

* `color` based on continent
* `size` based on population
* fixed transparency at 50%

Using the data, we have managed to draw a [**four-variable in a 2D plot**]{.hl-yellow}: `lifeExp` and `gdpPercap` on the axes, `continent` as color, and `pop` as the size of the geometry.

---

## Labs: labs()

We can also [**easily customize**]{.hl-yellow} using the `labs()` layer:

:::: columns
::: {.column width="43%"}

* `title, subtitle`
* `caption`
* `x, y`
* `size, color, fill, ...`: name in the legend for the **variables that encode** the different attributes


:::

::: {.column width="57%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp,
           color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida",
       y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente",
       size = "población")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp,
                 color = continent, size = pop),
             alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot", subtitle = "Datos de gapminder",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente", size = "población")
```

---

### [**Exercise 1**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Modify the `lifeExp` density plot we made earlier so that a separate density is drawn for each continent, with each continent having a different color. Also, set alpha to 50%, include a title, and translate all plot labels into Spanish.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_density(aes(x = lifeExp, fill = continent), alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Densidad",
       fill = "Continente", title = "Esperanza de vida por continente en 2007")
```


### [**Exercise 2**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Modify the `gdpPercap` boxplot to create the plot below, setting the alpha to 50%.


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.7
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(y = continent, x = gdpPercap, fill = continent),
               alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Renta per cápita", y = "Continentes",
       fill = "Continente", title = "Renta per cápita por continente en 2007")
```


### [**Exercise 3**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Explore the `geom_boxplot()` function to highlight outliers in `"darkred"` with a size of 3.5. Think about how you could hide the outliers.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(y = continent, x = gdpPercap, fill = continent),
               alpha = 0.5,  outlier.color = "darkred",
               outlier.size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Renta per cápita", y = "Continentes",
       fill = "Continente", title = "Renta per cápita por continente en 2007")

# sin outliers
ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(y = continent, x = gdpPercap, fill = continent),
               alpha = 0.5,  outliers = FALSE) +
  # o poniendo outlier.alpha = 0
  labs(x = "Renta per cápita", y = "Continentes",
       fill = "Continente", title = "Renta per cápita por continente en 2007")
```

### [**Exercise 4**]{.hl-yellow}

📝 Explore a bit the `geom_...()` functions (tab and see what comes up). After that, try to replicate the following plot, performing any operations you consider necessary (attention to the title and axes). For lines, line width is specified with `linewidth = ...`. Check `vignette("ggplot2-specs")` if you need it.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3
gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Africa") |>

```

# L2: [ggplot]{.flow} {#clase-1-2}



[**Customize your ggplot**]{style="color:#444442;"}

* [📆 Planning](#planificacion-2)


---

## Scale layer

So far, with `aes()` we have only mapped `aesthetic 1 → variable 1`
 or `aesthetic 2 → variable 2` but [**we haven’t been able to customize this mapping**]{.hl-red}.

* What colors do we want?
* If size depends on population, do we want it to range from a minimum to a maximum value?
* Do we want the X-axis in specific units?
* Do we want the Y-axis on a logarithmic scale?

. . .

One of the most important layers is [**scale (customization) layer**]{.hl-yellow} or `scale_...()`

---

## Scale layer: color/fill

Let’s customize colors with `scale_color_...()` and `scale_fill_...()`.

```{r}
gg_basics <-
  ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 3) 
```

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size:70%"}

With `scale_color_manual(values = ...)` we can manually specify a [**palette**]{.hl-yellow} by passing colors as a vector.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
pal <- c("#A02B85", "#2DE86B", "#4FB2CA", "#E8DA2D", "#E84C2D")
gg_basics +
  scale_color_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot", caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```

:::
::::
      
```{r}
#| eval: false
gg_basics +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#A02B85", "#2DE86B", "#4FB2CA", "#E8DA2D", "#E84C2D")) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

---

## Scale layer: color/fill


Another option is to choose one of the [**pre-designed color palettes**]{.hl-yellow} from packages like `{ggthemes}`.

:::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}


* `scale_color_colorblind()`: palette of colors adapted for  [**colorblind people**]{.hl-yellow}.

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggthemes)
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```


:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ggthemes)
gg_basics +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot", caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```



---

## Scale layer: color/fill

We can even load [**color palettes inspired by movies or art**]{.hl-yellow}.

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

* [**paintings**]{.hl-yellow}: the `{MetBrewer}` package (GitHub repository BlakeRMills/MetBrewer

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(MetBrewer)
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = met.brewer("Monet")) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot", caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
devtools::install_github(repo = "BlakeRMills/MetBrewer") 
library(MetBrewer)
gg_basics +
  scale_color_manual(values = met.brewer("Monet")) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```


---


## Scale layer: color/fill

We can even load [**color palettes inspired by movies or art**]{.hl-yellow}.

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

* [**albums**]{.hl-yellow}: the `{peRReo}` package (GitHub repository `jbgb13/peRReo`) using `scale_colour_manual(values = latin_palette()`).

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(peRReo)
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = latin_palette("rosalia")) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
devtools::install_github(repo = "jbgb13/peRReo") 
library(peRReo)

gg_basics +
  scale_color_manual(values = latin_palette("rosalia")) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```

## Scale layer: color gradient

We have already seen how to define color palettes, but if you notice, the variable encoding the color was qualitative or discrete. **What if the variable encoding color were quantitative numeric?**

. . . 

There are some color palettes known as **ColorBrewer** that can be defined as sequential, diverging, or qualitative (see info at <https://colorbrewer2.org>).

```{r}
RColorBrewer::brewer.pal.info
```

---

## Scale layer: color gradient

With `RColorBrewer::brewer.pal()` we can get a vector of n colors for a given palette, for example the **diverging palette** `RdYlBu`.

```{r}
RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n = 5, name = "RdYlBu")
```

. . .

With `RColorBrewer::display.brewer.pal()` we can **visualize the colors from the palette**.

```{r}
RColorBrewer::display.brewer.pal(n = 10, name = "RdYlBu")
```

---


## Scale layer: color gradient


An example of **sequential palette** is `PuBuGn`


```{r}
RColorBrewer::display.brewer.pal(n = 8, name = "PuBuGn")
```

---

## Scale layer: color gradient


An example of **qualitative palette** is

```{r}
RColorBrewer::display.brewer.pal(n = 8, name = "Pastel1")
```


---


## Scale layer: color gradient

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

To include it, we can use `scale_color_brewer()` or `scale_color_distiller()` if we want to **create a real continuous scale (interpolating between the colors)**.

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = pop, color = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "RdYlBu") +
  labs(x = "Población", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "esperanza de vida") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = pop, color = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "RdYlBu") +
  labs(x = "Población", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "esperanza de vida") +
  theme_minimal()
```


---

## Scale layer: color gradient

We can also create [**custom color gradients**]{.hl-yellow} with `scale_color_gradient()`, `scale_fill_gradient()`, `scale_color_gradient2()`, `scale_fill_gradient2()`.


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size:80%"}

We are going to use `scale_color_gradient2(low = ..., mid = ..., high = ..., midpoint = ...)`, specifying the lowest and highest colors, as well as the middle color (and the numeric value we want to associate with it).

:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = pop, color = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "#825598", mid = "#9dd0c1", high = "#d93535", midpoint = 60) +
  labs(x = "Población", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "esperanza de vida") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = pop, color = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "#825598", mid = "#9dd0c1", high = "#d93535", midpoint = 60) +
  labs(x = "Población", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "esperanza de vida") +
  theme_minimal()
```


---

## Scale layer: axis

The **same idea** we used to customize colors can be applied, for example, to [**customize the axes**]{.hl-yellow} using `scale_x_...()` and `scale_y_...()`.

:::: columns

::: {.column width="47%"}

Let’s [**customize the x-axis ticks**]{.hl-yellow} using `scale_x_continuous(breaks = ...)` to have breaks every 10 units.

:::

::: {.column width="53%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 90, by = 10)) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
gg_basics +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 90, by = 10)) +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```


---

## Scale layer: axis

Let’s dive a bit deeper into the [**scales**]{.hl-yellow} within our scatter plot

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

In `scale_x_continuous()` and `scale_y_continuous()`, in addition to setting breaks, we can also [**fix axis limits**]{.hl-purple} using `limits = ....`

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(50, 70),
                     breaks = seq(50, 70, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1000, 18000),
                      breaks = seq(0, 18000, by = 1000)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

:::

::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
gg_basics +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(50, 70),
                     breaks = seq(50, 70, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1000, 18000),
                     breaks = seq(0, 18000, by = 1000)) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") 
```

---

## Scale layer: axis


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

* How can we [**label axis units**]{.hl-purple}? Using the `{scales}` package, we can add [**prefixes/suffixes**]{.hl-yellow} with `labels = label_number(...)`.

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(scales)
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(50, 70), breaks = seq(50, 70, by = 5),
                     labels = label_number(suffix = " años")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1000, 18000), breaks = seq(0, 18000, by = 1000),
                     labels = label_number(suffix = " $")) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(scales)
gg_basics +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(50, 70),
                     breaks = seq(50, 70, by = 5),
                     labels = label_number(suffix = " años")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1000, 18000),
                     breaks = seq(0, 18000, by = 1000),
                     labels = label_number(suffix = " $")) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

---

## Scale layer: axis


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

* How can we [**change size, alpha, and other settings**]{.hl-purple}? Just like we have `scale_x_...()` or `scale_color_...()`, we also have `scale_size_...()` and `scale_alpha_...()`.


:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = pop)) +
  scale_size(range = c(4, 12)) +
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.1, 0.95)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       subtitle = "Alpha depends on population. guides(alpha = 'none') to remove it from the legend",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
gg_basics +
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.1, 0.5)) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       subtitle = "Alpha depends on population. guides(alpha = 'none') to remove it from the legend",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```

---

## Scale layer: axis


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

* How can we [**change the (linear) scale relationship between axes**]{.hl-purple}? With `scale_x_sqrt()` or `scale_x_log10()` we can modify the axis scale (without modifying the data!)

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente")
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
gg_basics +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita",
       title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana",
       color = "continente")
```

## Stats layer


Una capa también importante es la [**capa de estadísticas**]{.hl-yellow} con `stat_...()`

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}


* `stat_smooth()`: visualiza un [**ajuste suavizado**]{.hl-yellow} de los datos (reg. lineal, glm, loess, gam, etc). Con `stat_smooth(method = "lm")` una recta de regresión, con `stat_smooth(method = "loess")` un ajuste local polinomial

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent, size = pop), alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::
::::


```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent, size = pop), alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

Fíjate que si usas en la [**primera capa parámetros estéticos**]{.hl-yellow} se acaban [**heredando a capas posteriores**]{.hl-purple}, en concreto al ajuste visualizado.

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
  scale_y_log10() +

  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +

```
:::

```{r}

  scale_y_log10() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
```

## Stats layer

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

Dentro de `stat_smooth()` podemos especificarle otro [**ajuste polinómico**]{.hl-yellow} dándole expresión en `formula = ...`, por ejemplo un **polinomio de grado 5** `formula = y ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3) + I(x^4) + I(x^5)`
:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent, size = pop), alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3) + I(x^4) + I(x^5),
              color = "firebrick", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::
::::


```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent, size = pop), alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3) + I(x^4) + I(x^5),
              color = "firebrick", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```


---

## Stats layer



:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

Con `stat_summary()` podemos incluso añadir [**estadísticas por grupos**]{.hl-yellow}, como la media o mediana.

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = year)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7, alpha = 0.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", size = 0.4, color = "coral") + 
  stat_summary(fun = "median", size = 0.4, color = "darkcyan") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::


```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = year)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7, alpha = 0.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", size = 0.4, color = "coral") + 
  stat_summary(fun = "median", size = 0.4, color = "darkcyan") +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Facet layer

The `facet_()` layer allows us to [**split the plots (facet) by groups**]{.hl-yellow}, equivalent to `group_by()` in the tidyverse.


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

For example, let’s create a [**plot by continent**]{.hl-yellow}, showing all the plots at once (but separately) using `facet_wrap(~continent)`.

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~continent)+
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~continent) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Facet layer


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

By default, the scales on the axes are shared. If we want the [**axis scales to vary independently**]{.hl-yellow}, we should use `scales = "free_x"`, `scales = "free_y"`, or `scales = "free"`.



:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~continent, scales = "free") +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp,
           size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~continent, scales = "free") +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Facet layer

:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

With `nrow = ...` and `ncol = ...` we can [**specify how many rows and columns**]{.hl-yellow} we want in the grid of plots.


:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~continent, scales = "free", nrow = 3) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp,
           size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_wrap(~continent, scales = "free", nrow = 3) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Facet layer


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

We can also pass two arguments (variables) to [**create a grid of plots**]{.hl-yellow} with `facet_grid(var1 ~ var2)`

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder |> filter(year >= 1962), aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  facet_grid(continent ~ year, scales = "free") +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
ggplot(gapminder |>
         filter(year >= 1962),

  facet_grid(continent ~ year, scales = "free") +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Theme layer

Finally, the [**theme**]{.hl-yellow}. In `{ggplot2}` we can [**customize the entire plot**]{.hl-yellow}, including defining our own aesthetic theme by using the `theme_...()` layers. 



:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

For example, we will use `theme_minimal()` to have a “clean” and minimalist theme (we will learn how to define every detail).

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(35, 85, by = 10)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(35, 85, by = 10)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Theme layer


:::: columns

::: {.column width="45%"}

With theme() we can customize everything in the plot, for example the position of the legend and the typography of the X-axis titles.

:::


::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(35, 85, by = 10)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", 
        axis.title.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13))
```

:::
::::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(gapminder_2007, aes(y = gdpPercap, x = lifeExp, color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(35, 85, by = 10)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Esperanza de vida", y = "Renta per cápita", title = "Primer ggplot",
       caption = "J. Álvarez Liébana", color = "continente") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", 
        axis.title.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13))
```

## Join plots: patchwork


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
gg1 <-
  ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = pop, color = continent)) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_minimal()
gg2 <- 
  ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_density(aes(x = lifeExp, color = continent, fill = continent),
               alpha = 0.5) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  ggthemes::scale_fill_colorblind() +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_minimal()
gg3 <- 
  ggplot(gapminder_2007) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = continent, y = gdpPercap, color = continent, fill = continent),
               alpha = 0.5) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  ggthemes::scale_fill_colorblind() +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
library(patchwork)
(gg1 + (gg2 / gg3))
```
